seed.title: Speculative decoding with a tiny draft model so…
seed.prompt: Speculative decoding with a tiny draft model so a 7B LLM runs noticeably faster on a single RTX 4090, without retraining the big model

flower.idea: Measure when speculative decoding with a tiny same-tokenizer draft model speeds up a 7B Q4 GGUF on one RTX 4090 in llama.cpp, lossless and with no retraining. The core is a small comparison of no speculation, tiny draft and draft-free n-gram lookup on three prompt sets (code edit, summarization, chat), logging tok/s, acceptance and VRAM to a shared JSON schema with the paired-median method. A cheap n-gram hit-rate probe on the prompt is tested as a mode chooser. A one-page React/D3 explainer, with sliders for acceptance, draft length and cost ratio, overlays the measured points on the predicted speedup curve and shows a per-token accept/reject strip. The explainer can start on mock data in weekend 1 and swap in real logs later.

findings.text: llama.cpp benchmark methodology on a single RTX 4090 already exists (paired-median, acceptance rate), but for a 27B target with MTP and n-gram, not a tiny draft on a dense 7B. The method is reusable but the numbers do not transfer.

directions.title: Tiny Draft vs N-gram: Hybrid Chooser on 4090
directions.pitch: On one 7B Q4 GGUF, compare a tiny same-tokenizer draft, llama.cpp n-gram lookup and no speculation across three prompt sets of about 20 prompts. Log tok/s, acceptance and VRAM with the paired-median method, then test whether an n-gram hit-rate probe beats the best fixed mode. Do this first, because it produces the data for the explainer.
directions.why_you: It uses llama.cpp and Python, starts from simple baselines, fits 8 h/week on one 4090, and gives you the efficient-inference result you care about.

directions.title: Interactive Draft-Length Explainer with Measured 4090 Points
directions.pitch: Build a static React/D3 page with sliders for acceptance, draft length and cost ratio. It plots measured points over the predicted speedup curve and shows one real accept/reject strip. Start with mock data against the shared JSON schema so it never waits on the benchmark.
directions.why_you: It plays to your React and data-viz skills and your liking for visual explanations, and the formula is simple enough to finish in small steps.

handoff.objective: On one RTX 4090, measure when lossless speculative decoding with a tiny same-tokenizer draft model (or draft-free n-gram lookup) speeds up a 7B Q4 GGUF in llama.cpp with no retraining. Then show the results in a one-page React/D3 explainer with measured points overlaid on the predicted speedup curve.
handoff.metric: Decode tokens/s of the best speculative mode divided by no-speculation tokens/s (paired median, greedy, identical outputs), reported per task type (code edit, summarization, chat). Maximize. Acceptance rate and peak VRAM are logged as secondary numbers.
handoff.baseline: llama.cpp with no speculation on the chosen 7B Q4 GGUF, greedy decoding, same prompts and same output length. Next baseline: llama.cpp n-gram lookup (draft-free, no extra VRAM; see zero-vram-spec, src_8321a05f). Reuse the paired-median method from kuotunyu/qwen38-speculative-decoding-benchmark (src_57b250f5).

Draft length / max draft tokens and min acceptance probability flags
The probe rule: n-gram hit-rate threshold and probe length
Own benchmark script, prompt files and the explainer's React/D3 code
Log files that follow the JSON schema

handoff.background: No source reports tiny-draft numbers for a dense 7B on a 4090, so those results are unknown until measured. The closest runtime and GPU match is kuotunyu/qwen38-speculative-decoding-benchmark (src_57b250f5), which uses a 27B target with MTP and n-gram. It gives a reusable paired-median and acceptance method, but its numbers do not transfer. Harness references are amagilabs/amagi-draftbench (src_8cbd221e), which sweeps drafts and n-gram lookup and reports tok/s, acceptance and VRAM, and amanzainal/specdecode-roi (src_c1cacee9), which sweeps draft length and finds break-even. The paper "A Sparse Glimpse of the Whole: Train-Free Self-Speculative Decoding" (src_ea354241) gives a speedup model: longer speculation hurts when acceptance falls below relative drafting cost. That model drives the explainer's sliders and is checked against the measured runs. zero-vram-spec (src_8321a05f) is the draft-free n-gram reference. Overlap with src_1c50a8d8 is unverified, so the novelty claim is tentative.
preferences: Small steps, with one thing working before the next starts
Visual explanations: plots and the explainer page matter, not only tables
Python and PyTorch for scripts, React for the page; Rust and CUDA are optional learning goals and are not needed here

smoke.assumption: The speculative decoding speedup formula can be computed from mock JSON in an agreed schema and yields a sensible curve over acceptance and draft length.
smoke.rationale: The explainer depends on the formula and the JSON schema being consistent before building any React UI. This checks both cheaply. Cost model: expected tokens per round = (1-a^(k+1))/(1-a), cost per round = k*c + 1, speedup = tokens/cost. I did not verify this against src_ea354241 and the check does not either; that comparison is still to do.
smoke.code:
import json, math

def speedup(a, k, c):
    tokens = (1 - a**(k+1)) / (1 - a) if a < 1 else k + 1
    cost = k * c + 1
    return tokens / cost
